parts.title: Finding a two-dimensional doughnut-shaped map inside the brain's grid cells, even while an animal runs along a single straight line
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Some experiments are very simple. One example is a rat whose head is held still while it runs on a wheel. Another is sleep. Simple experiments are easy to run, but they show the animal doing only a few things, so it is hard to tell which kinds of brain cells do which jobs. Grid cells are a good example. These brain cells fire in a striking repeating pattern, like tiles on a floor. We think they would never have been discovered without watching animals move freely in an open space.

Here we show that if we stop looking at one brain cell at a time and start looking at groups of cells together, we can get away with much simpler experiments. We find groups of grid cells, called grid cell modules. We then show that their activity fills the same steady, doughnut-shaped space, which we call a torus, while the animal runs on a wheel as it does while it searches for food in an open box. The paths the activity traces around this doughnut match single runs in a virtual reality setup, and they also match path integration in the dark. Path integration means working out where you are by adding up your own movements, without using landmarks. When we change the conditions of the experiment, the way the activity lines up with the animal's position shifts quickly.

This gives us a way to discover and study complicated maps inside the brain, even in the simplest experiments.

Subject terms: Neural circuits, Neural decoding
parts.introduction_first:
In neuroscience, researchers now study many more brain cells at once, and they watch animals do more varied, more natural things. Experiments have also moved from simple setups with only a few measured quantities to richer, more realistic behavior. Because of this, we need better assumptions and better ways of thinking to pull useful lessons out of these ever-growing piles of data.

One promising approach is called topological data analysis. Instead of trying to fit the data to a ready-made mathematical model, it looks for the shapes hidden in the data. It treats each measurement as a point in a cloud of points and asks what shapes that cloud has, such as loops or holes.

We build on this way of thinking and follow two main principles. First, we argue for a minimal approach to finding population codes in brain recordings. A population code is the way a group of brain cells together carries information. We want to uncover the patterns built into the cells themselves. We do not want to use what we already know about the task to decide which cells matter, or to tell the cells in advance what calculation they are doing. Second, we propose that the number of dimensions in a population code is not limited to the number of dimensions in the task. Instead, the code follows the brain's own internal structure, even in the simplest experiments.

We focus on one classic example: how rats and mice represent space. We find that even the simplest experiment can teach us about the basic calculations the brain carries out. This approach makes studying these brain codes simpler and wider, and it opens new paths to understanding more complex thinking abilities.
parts.introduction_rest:
Grid cells give us a fascinating glimpse into how the brain does its calculations. These cells are usually found in two-dimensional (2-D) environments, such as an open box, where an animal can move in any direction. They are known for their typical six-sided, or hexagonal, patterns, which help the animal find its way around. In earlier work, we found that groups of grid cells, called grid cell modules, form a doughnut-shaped map. This describes the two repeating directions of the grid pattern in 2-D environments.

On a single straight track, which is a one-dimensional (1-D) path, scientists have thought that grid cells simply respond to the animal's position along the track. In other words, they have thought of these responses as slices cut across the 2-D patterns. However, assuming that the map inside the brain is the same as the map outside it may be misleading. Recent results suggest that (putative) grid cells on 1-D tracks are tuned to integrated distance, meaning the total distance the animal has travelled, and are only weakly anchored to landmarks. Here, we asked whether studying the brain cells' activity on its own would let us find grid cell modules and describe the calculations they carry out, even when we change the conditions of the experiment and the way it is run.

A common way to study groups of brain cells starts by shrinking the data down to fewer dimensions. For example, researchers use a method called uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP), or latent variable models, including deep ones. The goal is to squeeze the activity of the whole group of cells at each moment into a small number of dimensions. However, this kind of shrinking requires choosing a range of settings and a way to start the method, called the initialization. In particular, researchers often choose a space with 2 or 3 dimensions because it is easy to understand. This lets them draw pictures of the data, but it may throw away important information.

Topological data analysis offers another way to describe clouds of points, even when they have many dimensions. It uses a tool called persistent homology. Persistent homology builds a series of spaces, one inside another, ordered by how strongly points are linked to each other. As it goes, it shows how holes of any size change over time. The result is a collection of time intervals, showing when each hole appears and when it disappears. This collection is called a barcode. The barcode helps us spot the main shapes in the data, such as loops, which are holes with one dimension.

However, persistent homology has weaknesses. It is sensitive to unusual points that sit far from the rest, and to data that only partly or unevenly covers the full range of possible states. When the activity of different groups of cells gets mixed together, it can also distort or complicate the shapes underneath. Persistent homology also has a computing bottleneck: the time it takes and the memory it needs grow quickly as the number of points in the cloud increases. So, to read the shapes from the barcodes, we need to prepare the data first. This means removing noise, keeping only a sample of the points, and separating the neurons into distinct groups.
parts.methods:
## Methods

### Preparing the brain recordings

We did not record any new data ourselves. Instead, we used recordings from earlier experiments. In one of them, Gardner and colleagues [59] used Neuropixels probes [60,61], which are thin silicon chips that record from many brain cells at once. They recorded from the MEC-parasubiculum, a region of the brain that contains grid cells. They did this in three male Long Evans rats, which we call 'R', 'S' and 'Q'. The rats were recorded while they slept and while they searched for food freely in two arenas: a square measuring 1.5 m × 1.5 m, and a wagon-wheel-shaped arena.

We used the spike times from two of these rats, 'R' and 'S'. A spike time is the moment when a cell fires. The spikes had already been sorted by cell using a program called KiloSort 2.5 [60]. In the original papers, grid cells were picked out by looking at each cell's spatial autocorrelogram. This is a map that shows how often a cell fires at the same place again and again, which reveals its repeating pattern. We used 483 grid cells from rat 'R' and 140 from rat 'S', during both open-field sessions and sleep.

In a similar way, Waaga and colleagues [62] used Neuropixels probes to record from the MEC of four Long Evans rats. The rats searched freely in a round arena 175 cm across, both in the dark and in the light. We used the spike times from 186 grid cells in rat 26018, which had been sorted and identified in the same way as above.

Next, we turned each spike time into a delta function. This is a spike that is 1 at the moment the cell fires and 0 at all other times. We then smoothed each spike with a Gaussian kernel, a bell-shaped curve that spreads the spike over a short stretch of time. The width of this curve, written σ, was 60 ms for the shape analysis and 100 ms for grouping cells in rats 'R' and 'S'. For rat 26018, it was 100 ms for the shape analysis and 500 ms for grouping cells. Adding up all the smoothed spikes gave a smooth firing rate for each cell, meaning how fast it was firing at each moment.

We sampled these firing rates every 10 ms for rat 26018, every 20 ms for rat 'R' and every 50 ms for rat 'S', for the shape analysis. For grouping cells, we sampled every 100 ms. We then took the square root of each firing rate. This stops a few very active cells from dominating. We grouped the cells into groups of grid cells, and we analyzed each group separately (see 'Finding groups of grid cells' below). For rats 'R' and 'S', we used a cut-off of ρ = 0.4 r, and for the dark session of rat 26018, ρ = 0.89 r. We set the maximum time lag, τmax, to 3 s.

We then removed moments when the animal was not moving. For this, we filtered the firing rates by speed, keeping only moments when the animal moved at least 5 cm per second for rat 26018 and 10 cm per second for rats 'R' and 'S'.

After that, we used a method called PCA whitening. PCA (principal component analysis) finds the main directions in which a set of data varies. Whitening then rescales the data so that each of these directions has the same size, which removes noise. We applied it to the data from all the cells together, which we call the population vector. Here n is the number of cells. We first turned each cell's firing rate into a z-score, which means subtracting its average and dividing by its spread. We then projected these population vectors onto the first d = 6 directions for rat 26018 and d = 8 for rats 'R' and 'S'. Finally, we divided by the square root of the eigenvalues, which are numbers that describe how much each direction varies (see [34] for a thorough discussion of PCA as a way to prepare data).

Calculating barcodes, which we explain below, takes a lot of computing power. So we first shrank the point cloud, the cloud of points that each recording session produces, in two steps. We used the settings ϵ = 0.8, κ = 1000 and m = 2200 / 2100 for rats 'R' / 'S', and ϵ = 0.5 and m = 2000 for rat 26018 (see 'Shrinking the point cloud' below). Finally, we applied persistent homology (PH), a method that finds the shapes in the data. We measured how far apart two points were using the cosine distance, which compares the directions of two population vectors. We also used Z47 coefficients [47]. We chose 47 because it is unlikely to divide the torsion subgroup [37], a technical detail about the kinds of holes the method can detect.

To compare the data in 3-D pictures, we used a method called UMAP. It draws a flat picture in which points that are close in the data stay close. We applied it to the PCA-whitened firing rates of rat 'R' (d = 8), using the default settings, with 100 neighbors. We fitted it to two sets of data. The first was 20681 randomly drawn samples from the whole grid cell population. The second was the same number of samples from the activity of the group of grid cells, after the first shrinking step described above. We also fitted a method called CEBRA to the same data. CEBRA finds a way of describing the data that keeps the most important patterns. We used a batch size of 128 and one of two settings: "model_architecture = offset1-model" with cosine distance, or "offset-model-mse" with Euclidean distance.

Obenhaus and colleagues [40] recorded calcium in the MEC of adult male mice. They used a tiny two-photon microscope, similar to the one used in [41], which records the glow of a dye that lights up when calcium flows into a cell. The mice moved freely in an open field of 80 × 80 cm². The calcium traces were turned into calcium events, which are short bursts of activity (for details, see the Supplementary Information in [40]). We used the events from two mice, 88529 and 90222. The sessions were '26fd0fbe1e205255' (named '#1 W'), '1f20835f09e28706' ('#1 OF'), '419c1c6b319d0ddf' ('#2 W'), '5b92b96313c3fc19' ('#2 OF'), 'd5a06b6a7630bb11' ('#3 W'), '7e888f1d8eaab46b' ('#3 OF') and '5116e01aa80b6402'. We took them from the '__filtered_spikes' table in the MySQL database file 'dump.sql' (available in [63]).

We used the 'filtered_cells' table to get the cell IDs whose signal-to-noise ratio was above 3.5 (see the Supplementary Information in [40]). The signal-to-noise ratio tells us how strong a cell's signal is compared with the background noise.

For each cell, we rescaled the events to run from 0 to 1, smoothed them with a Gaussian kernel of σ = 0.27 s, and took the square root. We found groups of grid cells using both the open-field and wheel sessions, with ρ = 0.835 r for mouse 88529 and ρ = 0.91 r for mouse 90222, and τmax = 1.35 s. We filtered the data by speed, keeping only moments when the mouse moved at least 5 cm per second, and left out population vectors with no activity. We then applied the same steps as above, with d = 6 for mouse 88529 and d = 4 for mouse 90222, ϵ = 0.5 and 0.2, and m = 1200 and 600.

We also used a new, very small two-photon device called MINI2P. It recorded from 3 male and 2 female transgenic mice, which carry an added gene, and from 5 male wild-type mice, which are ordinary mice. The mice were 12-24 weeks old when they had surgery [41]. The implants were placed in the MEC, the hippocampus or the visual cortex. Recordings were made during an open-field task (a square box of 80 cm²), a ladder-climbing task and an escape task, and the calcium signals were turned into calcium events.

Here, we used only the calcium events from the 'NAT.mat' files of mouse 97045, day 20210307 (open-field session), which are available in [64]. We removed cells that were listed twice in the 'RepeatCell' variable of the matching 'NeuronInformation.mat' file. The neurons were recorded in two separate planes, with a time offset between them. So we filled in the activity at matching frames using the tool 'scipy.stats.interp1d'. We then set activity values below 10⁻¹⁰ to 0, and left out neurons whose average activity was above 10. This left 1-hour recordings of n = 350 neurons for mouse 97045. We used the same steps as for the calcium recordings above, with ρ = 0.85 r, d = 6, ϵ = 0.5 and m = 1600.

All of these experiments were carried out following the Norwegian Animal Welfare Act and the European Convention for the Protection of Vertebrate Animals used for Experimental and Other Scientific Purposes.

Campbell and colleagues recorded from the MEC, the retrosplenial cortex and the primary visual cortex of 32 female mice using Neuropixels probes. The mice ran on a wheel with their heads held still, in the dark, and while following a virtual reality setup (see Fig. 3a). The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Stanford University School of Medicine approved all the methods. We analyzed the spike times from a total of 119 sessions (all MEC recordings), which had been sorted using Kilosort 2 and are available in [65].

We turned each spike time into a delta function (1 at the moment of firing, 0 otherwise) and smoothed it with a Gaussian kernel of σ = 100 ms. Adding up all the spikes for each cell then gave a smooth firing rate. We sampled the firing rates every 10 ms (every 100 ms for grouping cells) and took the square root. We left out neurons that were not judged 'good' in one recording, based on contamination, signal-to-noise ratio and firing rate (see the Method details in [14]). We also left out neurons with average firing rates below 0.05 Hz or above 10 Hz.

We then grouped the remaining neurons (see 'Finding groups of grid cells'), using ρ = 0.46 r and τmax = 0.9 s, and using all available recordings: baseline, dark and gain/contrast sessions. We used the same steps as above, with d = 7, ϵ = 0.7 and m = 1200 for all groups.

Peyrache and colleagues recorded electrical signals from the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and the postsubiculum of 5 adult male and 2 female mice, using Neuronexus silicon probes [43]. The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of New York University Medical Center approved all the experiments. We used the same approach as above on the spike times of mouse 28, day 140313 (n = 62 neurons, sorted using KlustaKwik [66]), which are available in [67]. The data contained a 192-minute recording during wakefulness, rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep and slow-wave (SWS) sleep.

We analyzed the slow-wave sleep activity in the same way as described above. First, we smoothed one spike per spike with a Gaussian kernel of σ = 1 s for wake and REM sleep recordings, and σ = 0.5 s for slow-wave sleep. We then sampled the population vectors every 300 ms (for the shape analysis) and every 100 ms (for grouping cells), and took the square root. We grouped the neurons using all sessions, with ρ = 0.6 r and τmax = 3 s. We set ϵ = 0.1, d = 3 and m = 700. This gave barcodes showing a ring shape (Supplementary Fig. 1a.iii).

### Shrinking the point cloud

To cut down the computing work and to remove outliers, which are points far away from the rest, we shrank the point cloud before applying persistent homology. First, we used a 'radial' shrinking method, similar to the one in [1]. We chose the point with the largest absolute summed value as the first landmark point, and measured the Euclidean distance from it to all the other points. We threw away points closer than ϵ. Then we picked the remaining point that was closest to all the sampled landmark points, meaning the one with the largest distance to all landmarks. We repeated this until no points were left, which greatly reduced the size of the point cloud, leaving about 30–50% of the points. This method keeps the spread of the data, but it tends to keep outliers. So we then used a second method, based on how crowded the data is, called 'Fuzzy downsampling' (as in [4]), which we describe below.

Given a point cloud X, and for each point x in X a set Nx of its κ closest neighbors, we define for each x a membership function μx: X → I, where I = [0, 1]. This function gives each point a score between 0 and 1 for how strongly it belongs to the neighborhood of x:

(1) μx(y) = exp(−d(x, y) / σx),

where d(x, y) is the distance between points x and y. We choose σx so that the scores of all the neighbors add up to log2(k):

∑y∈Nx μx(y) = log2(k).

We then built a global membership function μ(x, y) that combines the scores from both sides:

(2) μ(x, y) = μx(y) + μy(x) − μx(y)μy(x).

We start with an empty set X0. Then we build a smaller set XN ⊂ X step by step, as follows.

In each step n > 0, we define a function Fn that adds up the membership scores of each point in the remaining point cloud x ∈ X′ = X \ Xn:

(3) Fn(x) = Σy∈X′ μ(x, y) = Σy∈X μ(x, y) − Σy∈Xn μ(x, y).

The (n + 1)-th point is then the point with the highest score:

(4) xn+1 = x that maximizes Fn(x).

In other words, the method keeps, one at a time, the point that is most likely to be in the neighborhoods of all the other points.

If we define μ(x, y) = exp(−d(x, y) / σy), this method is closely related to mean-shift clustering [68] and to the objective function used in the topological denoising technique introduced by Kloke and Carlsson [36]. That technique uses this function to move a smaller set of points to positions that reveal the true shapes. It describes this as a weighted difference of two Gaussian kernel density estimators, which are smooth maps of where the points are crowded. One is for the whole dataset X, and it pushes the smaller set XN towards the crowded regions of X. The other is for the smaller set itself, and it pushes the points away from each other. In the same way, fuzzy downsampling picks points from the crowded regions of X, but steers away from the regions already chosen.

### Persistent homology

We described the shape of the neural data using persistent cohomology. This gives the same barcodes as persistent homology (which we describe below), but cohomology was needed to read off the map [37].

The homology of a topological space T is a sequence of vector spaces Hn(T), for all natural numbers n ∈ N. The rank of Hn(T) tells us how many n-dimensional holes there are [69]. A zero-dimensional hole is a connected component, a 1-dimensional hole is a circle, a 2-dimensional hole is a void, and so on for higher dimensions. The homology of a point cloud X only counts the points. So, to find holes that reflect the space the data was sampled from, we attach combinatorial spaces called Rips complexes, Tτ(X), to the data. A Rips complex is a network of points joined by lines when they are close enough. It depends on a scale τ, which usually describes how far apart two points can be and still count as close. Changing τ gives an ordered sequence of complexes, called the Rips filtration:

(5) Tτ0 ⊂ Tτ1 ⊂ … ⊂ Tτn,

where τ0 < τ1 < … < τn. Applying homology to this sequence gives a sequence of vector spaces and maps, for each dimension n:

(6) Hn(Tτ0(X)) → Hn(Tτ1(X)) → … → Hn(Tτn(X)).

The whole collection of sequences is called persistent homology, PH*(X). It can be broken down into a sum of simple persistence intervals, I([bi, di)):

(7) PHn(X) ≅ ⨁i I([bi, di)).

Here, bi < di gives the scales at which an n-dimensional hole in PHn(X) first appears and later disappears. Persistent homology can therefore be drawn as bars, starting at bi and ending at di. The collection of such bars, across all dimensions, is called the barcode.

To get a shuffled distribution of barcodes, we randomly shifted the activity of each neuron by a random amount of time. We then applied the same steps to the shuffled population activity to get a barcode. We repeated this 100 times, each time with a different random seed.

We used the program Ripser [70,71] for all calculations of persistent cohomology.

### Reading off the map from the activity

We used circular coordinates, as introduced by De Silva and colleagues [37], to study how the population activity changes over time. This method has been used before to study head direction and grid cell activity [1,4]. It is based on a theoretical link between 1-D cohomology and maps from a topological space to a circle.

We took the n longest-lived H1 bars in the barcode, which are the bars for 1-dimensional holes that last longest. For each of them, we took the Rips complex at τ = b + 0.99 ⋅ (d − b), where b and d are the birth and death of the bar (see Supplementary Fig. 10b,c for how this choice affects reading off the map). We then calculated n-D toroidal coordinates for all the points in the Rips complex. For n = 1, this gives circular coordinates. We also decorated the circular coordinates (for n ≥ 2), as introduced by Scoccola and colleagues [72].

The points in the Rips complex are the m points in the shrunken point cloud, so we get only m toroidal coordinates. To extend these to the rest of the original point cloud, or to a different session, we first weighted the coordinates by the values of the matching points. This gave a distribution on the torus for each dimension. We then calculated the toroidal coordinates for each time step by weighting the distribution by the value of each point in the full point cloud, and finding the mass centers of the summed weighted distributions.

To show the read-off toroidal positions as the animal moved along the virtual reality track (Fig. 3h and Supplementary Fig. 5), we smoothed the coordinates over time with a Gaussian filter of σ = 0.5 s.

For the group of grid cells that codes for head direction, we used slow-wave sleep to read off the map for both awake and sleep data. To find which way the map was turned, we tried turning the read-off angles clockwise and anticlockwise. We fixed the starting point by choosing the turn that made the average difference to the recorded head direction angles during wake sessions as small as possible.

### Rate maps and autocorrelograms

We divided the positions in the open field into a grid of 302 squares, which gave us spatial rate maps. We calculated the average neural activity in each square and smoothed it with a Gaussian filter of width 2 squares. Squares the animal never visited were given the average value of the squares it did visit.

We also made 1-D spatial autocorrelograms for the positions on the running wheel and on the virtual reality track, using 1 cm and 4 cm squares, respectively. An autocorrelogram shows how similar a pattern is to a shifted copy of itself. For each cell, we found the average activity in each square and took the dot product between this and a copy of it with zeros added, shifting the copy by up to 300 squares.

We calculated toroidal firing rate maps in the same way as for the open-field arena. First, we divided the toroidal surface into a square grid of 12° × 12° squares and calculated the average activity in each square. To smooth the toroidal rate map, we had to deal with the 60° angle of the toroidal axes. So we first shifted the squares sideways by a length equal to half the squares' vertical position. To handle the edges, we then tiled nine copies of the shifted rate map and smoothed it as the open-field rate maps. We took out the middle tile and shifted it back. For the pictures, we gave the resulting rate maps shear angles of 15° both sideways and up and down.

We calculated the angular tuning curves, which show how a cell's activity changes with direction, using 60 squares and scaling them so that the highest value is 1.

For 3-D toroidal tuning, we first used radial shrinking of the coordinates (ϵ = 0.5) to get spherical squares, and colored each center point by the average value for each square.

### Finding groups of grid cells

We grouped the cells recorded electrically by how closely their activity matched over time. We measured this with the time-lag cross-correlation between each pair of cells, as in [73], for the whole population recording:

(8) cij(t′) = ∫0^T si(t) sj(t + t′) dt,

where si(t) is the firing rate of cell i at time t, turned from spike times as described in 'Preparing the brain recordings', using a Gaussian kernel of σ = 0.3 s and sampled every 30 ms. T is the total length of the recording. We then took the inverse, normalized cross-correlation, with τmax as given for each recording above:

(9) Cij = minτ cij(τ), cij(τ0) / τmax, maxτ cij(τ), cij(τ0) / τmax.

We wanted to stress that cells in the same group should match each other more strongly than they match other cells. So, for each cell, we took its squared cross-correlation with all other cells, averaged over all recordings of the same pair of cells, and turned these into a distance. We then used agglomerative clustering with average linkage on this distance, which joins the most similar cells and groups step by step. We used ρ as the distance cut-off (see above for the values of ρ). We threw away groups with fewer than 19 cells, because that is too few cells to be confident about the toroidal structure (see Supplementary Fig. 4e in [4]).

### Finding a hexagonal torus

To find out whether the read-off toroidal coordinates suggested a hexagonal torus in the virtual reality sessions, we modeled each cell's firing rates and rate maps. We compared them with the exact heat pattern on both a hexagonal and a square torus (Supplementary Fig. 3). The heat kernel on the hexagonal torus, with a heat source at the center, is given as:

(10) Hhex(x, y; t) = (1/t) Σ(k, l)∈Z² exp(−π(1/t)²/3 ((k + x)² + (k + x)(l + y) + (l + y)²)),

which describes the temperature at toroidal positions (x, y) ∈ [0, 1]² after time t. The heat kernel on the square torus [44] is:

(11) Hsqr(x, y; t) = (1/t) Σ(k, l)∈Z² exp(−π(1/t) ((k + x)² + (l + y)²)).

We tested how well the original toroidal rate maps for the virtual reality data fit a toroidal heat pattern from a single point source. We made these maps by calculating the average activity in 102 squares of the m toroidal coordinates found before extending them to the full point cloud (see 'Reading off the map from the activity').

First, we sampled m toroidal coordinates at even spacing. We moved the center of the sampled torus to each cell's peak activity on the torus, based on radial shrinking of the m original coordinates (see 'Comparing toroidal tuning'). Using t = 0.1 and k, l ∈ {−1, 0, 1} in the equations above, we could calculate a temperature estimate for each toroidal position. We defined the heat pattern on the sampled torus as the average temperature in 102 square squares. The straight-line correlation between the heat pattern and the firing rate maps confirmed the expected hexagonal toroidal tuning of each cell.

A hexagonal torus has three repeating axes, and we did not know in advance which pair of axes the read-off torus might describe. However, this shows up as a left or right 45° shift in the pattern. So we also tested the reversed orientation by reversing one of the sampled coordinates. We judged the fit by the highest correlation between the modeled rate maps and the original one, and compared it with a square torus rate map modeled in the same way. We required the median correlation of a group of cells to be above 0.6, and we classified it as a hexagonal torus. This rule of thumb avoids the hard computing problem of doing statistics on barcodes [74].

When we used the read-off toroidal positions instead of the sampled coordinates to calculate the heat kernel Hhex, we got heat models that change over time for each cell's firing rate. This let us calculate spatial autocorrelograms for idealized hexagonal toroidal tuning, which looked like the original firing rate maps (Supplementary Fig. 3d).

### Straightening out the torus and measuring path length

We smoothed the read-off coordinates with a 0.2 s Gaussian kernel and unwrapped them onto a flat space, to make it easier to study the paths the activity traces around the torus. To do this, we checked step by step whether the next toroidal coordinate crossed either of the two circular starting points (one for each dimension). We tried all combinations (0 or 1 crossings per circle), and chose the next point as the one closest to the previous one, measured by the Euclidean distance.

To see how changing the gain, which is how strongly the grid pattern is strengthened, affects the internal map, we measured the length of the straightened toroidal paths for each trial. First, we fitted a straight line to the positions for each axis, using linear regression. We only included paths with a fit above 0.5 r on both axes. We then measured the length of each trial as the Euclidean distance between the start and end points of the 2-D straight-line fit.

### Lining up the toroidal coordinates

When we read off the toroidal coordinates, we choose the starting point and the direction of the axes freely. So, to compare sessions, we first turned the read-off toroidal coordinates to match each other in pairs. We also had to allow for the hexagonal torus, which has three axes 60 or 120 degrees apart (Supplementary Fig. 10a).

For each lining-up, we kept one set of toroidal coordinates fixed. The goal was to give the second set the same direction and axes. In other words, the second set was the coordinates we got by reading off the first session using the torus found in the second session. We tested all possible combinations of directions and axes. For each combination, we smoothed the coordinates over time with a 1-D Gaussian filter of width 200 ms, calculated the average angular difference, and chose the combination with the smallest difference.

To line up the toroidal coordinates of the groups of grid cells with the 2-D open-field recordings, we chose the combination of axes and direction that looked most alike across different mice and sessions. We did this by reading off the open-field data and plotting the average toroidal coordinate in 302 square squares of the open-field coordinates (Fig. 2a).

### Comparing toroidal tuning

We compared the peak toroidal positions across sessions to see whether the toroidal tuning stayed the same. We found each cell's preferred location as the mass center of its activity on the torus (162 squares), given by:

(12) Tpeak = arctan2( Σi sin ϕi ⋅ si / Σi si, Σi cos ϕi ⋅ si / Σi si ),

where si is the average activity in the i-th toroidal square ϕi.

### Simulations of continuous attractor networks

To study the toroidal structure of grid cell continuous attractor network (CAN) models, we simulated the firing rates of three noiseless CAN models (Supplementary Fig. 3a). A continuous attractor network is a network of brain cells in which the activity can settle into a stable pattern that can move smoothly around a torus, like a map of the animal's position.

First, we simulated a 56 × 44 grid cell network with purely inhibitory connections, as proposed in [75]. To model the animal's behavior, we used the first 1000 s of the recorded path of rat 'R' during the open-field foraging session on day 1, found in [4]. We filled in the positions at 2 ms time steps and calculated the speed s(t) and head direction ϕ(t) from the difference in position between each time step. The firing rate at time step tn+1 was given as:

(13) f(tn+1) = f(tn) + (1/ρ) [−f(tn) + J+ f(tn) ⋅ W+ γ s(tn) cos(ϕ(tn) − ϕ̄)]+,

where [ … ]+ is the Heaviside function, which keeps positive values and sets negative values to zero. ϕ̄ is the preferred head direction, and the parameters were J = 1, γ = 0.15, l = 2, R = 20, W0 = −0.01 and ρ = 10. We started the activity pattern at random and let it settle by running the equation above 2000 times with no movement. We set the firing rate to 0 if it was below 0.0001, and resampled it at 10 ms time steps.

Next, we used the twisted torus model by Guanella and colleagues [45] to simulate a 20 × 20 grid cell network for a simulated random walk in a square box. The parameter definitions and code are in the open-source version by Santos Pata (https://github.com/DiogoSantosPata/gridcells). We used 5000 time frames and 'grid_gain=0.06'.

Finally, we used an untwisted version of the previous model, which made square grid cell patterns, for a 10 × 10 network. We simulated this with a Python version of the Matlab code by Zilli [76]. We used 20 ms time steps and simulated a total of 295 s, following an open-field path recorded by Hafting and colleagues [7], which is provided in the same code repository.

### Data analysis and statistics

We did all the data analyses with our own scripts in Python 3.9.12. We used the following open-source Python packages: umap (version 0.5.5), ripser (0.6.4), numba (0.58.1), scipy (1.11.4), numpy (1.26.2), scikit-learn (0.24.2), matplotlib (3.8.2), h5py (3.6.0), gtda (0.6.0), cv2 (4.8.1), pandas (1.4.2) and datajoint (0.13.5), IPython (8.2.0), Cebra (0.3.1).

We also used the open-source software Jupyter notebook 6.4.8 and MySQL 5.7.

We did most of the analyses on a Macbook Pro M2, macOS Ventura (13). The CEBRA calculations were done on a Lenovo Thinkpad, Intel i7, Windows 11.

The heaviest computing was done on the resources of the NTNU IDUN/EPIC computing cluster [77] and of the Department of Mathematical Sciences.

All our statistical tests were one-sided, meaning they looked for an effect in one direction only.

### Reporting summary

More information on how we designed the research is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

## Results

### Finding a group of cells that combines head direction and grid patterns

We start with a recording made by Gardner and colleagues (Fig. 1a; a similar analysis for another rat, 'S', is in Supplementary Fig. 1b). They used Neuropixels, a thin probe that records from hundreds of brain cells at once, to record 483 grid cells from rat 'R' in an open box. If we simply fed all of these grid cells into two common tools for flattening data into a picture, called UMAP and CEBRA, we got no shape we could make out (Fig. 1b, top).

So we sorted the cells into groups instead. We compared each pair of cells by how closely their firing patterns matched when one was shifted in time against the other. This is called a time-lagged cross-correlation. We then joined the most similar cells step by step, a method called agglomerative clustering. This gave us one clear group of cells (Fig. 1c).

The activity of this group, however, seemed to have more dimensions than we could draw on a flat page (Fig. 1b, bottom). So we turned to persistent homology, a method that finds loops and holes in a cloud of points. First, we used a step called PCA whitening on eight dimensions. This squeezes out the main information in the data (ref. 34). Next, we thinned out the data in two steps, based on how spread out and how crowded the points were (refs. 1, 35, 36). This gave a sample that still represents the space well (Fig. 1d).

When we applied persistent homology to this smaller dataset, we found three circular features in the barcode (Fig. 1e). A barcode is a picture that persistent homology produces. Its bars show how long each loop or hole lasts as the data are viewed at different scales. Looking at loops of higher dimension would show more, but it takes a lot of computing power and needs more cells to be confident (ref. 31).

We could still get a more detailed view by looking at single bars in the barcode. Each bar can be turned into a circle, which gives an angle to each point in the data (refs. 37, 38). Doing this for the three bars gave us three circles. Together they describe the data as a three-dimensional doughnut, which we call a 3-torus. We can then compare this with the things we actually measured: the animal's head direction and its position in a flat, two-dimensional space.

One circle lines up with the direction the animal's head points. The other two capture the two directions of the grid cells' six-sided pattern (Fig. 1f). We also drew the activity of single cells on the 3-torus, shown as a cube whose opposite sides join up. Each cell had a single, smooth, hill-shaped area of high activity, called a tuning field. This shows that each cell marks its own unique place in the space (Fig. 1g). Our approach can therefore find and describe the space used by a group of cells that combine head direction with grid patterns (refs. 31, 39).

**Fig. 1. Finding a three-dimensional doughnut-shaped map in a group of grid cells that also carry head direction.**

**a** Gardner and colleagues recorded 483 grid cells (ref. 4) in rat 'R'. Top: the activity of one grid cell in an open box. Bottom: the direction it prefers. **b** We flattened the activity of the whole grid cell population (483 cells, top row, randomly sampled) and of the group we found (75 cells, bottom row, after processing) into three dimensions. We used CEBRA (ref. 20) with cosine distance (left) and Euclidean distance (middle), and UMAP (ref. 16) with cosine distance (right). Colors show the head direction (HD) angle recorded at the same time, as on the color wheel. **c** A table of how different each pair of cells is, sorted by the groups found by hierarchical clustering. Each value is one minus the Pearson correlation of the firing rates of two cells, after shifting one in time against the other (color bar). The largest group ('M', 75 cells) is marked. **d** The spike trains of all grid cells can be written as a table X of size N × T (cells × time; left). Gray bars mark the times of spikes. The group's activity X′ (upper right) is a smaller part of X (fewer than N cells). It is then thinned out in time (bottom right, X″, fewer than T time points). **e** Barcode from applying persistent homology to the group's activity after thinning (as in d). Bars show how long 0-dimensional features (H0, points) and 1-dimensional features (H1, loops) last. Three circular features are found (ϕ1–3, arrows). The shaded region shows the 99th percentile of the shuffled data. **f** We turned the circular features in (e) into angles (cohomological coordinatization, ref. 37) and compared them with the measured quantities. They show head direction (HD, top) and position in space (bottom; color shows the cosine value of the decoding, 'dec'). **g** Eight examples (rows) of single cells' firing rates, scaled to the same range, plotted against position in space (left column, color bar), head direction (middle) and the three-dimensional doughnut-shaped space (right). Each side of the cube is one circle, as in f, and opposite sides join up. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Several step-by-step methods using persistent homology have been suggested (refs. 1–3). We want to stress three things they should do. They should split the recording into the groups of cells that matter. They should process the activity to suit each group. And they should use the information in the barcode directly to work out how the activity moves.

We could also first pick out cells that respond to something we already know about, such as head direction, and then study the shape of the space. This may also teach us something (Supplementary Fig. 9 shows early analyses of head direction cells, boundary vector cells and object vector cells). But such a known quantity may not always be available. So we show our approach on several datasets. It reveals the circle of directions used by boundary vector cells (ref. 40; Supplementary Fig. 1b). It reveals the doughnut shape of grid cells in calcium imaging recordings from the entorhinal cortex and the parasubiculum (ref. 41; Supplementary Fig. 1c). It separates three grid cell modules recorded at the same time in the dark (ref. 42; Supplementary Fig. 1d). And it finds the circle used by head direction cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus and the post-subiculum during slow-wave sleep (SWS) (ref. 43; Fig. 1e). Earlier methods have not succeeded on these (see, for example, Supplementary Fig. 11 in ref. 2). In short, our method finds shapes in brain recordings. It gives more insight into the brain's internal calculations without first linking them to outside measurements through the cells' tuning.

### Mouse grid cells in the entorhinal cortex show a doughnut-shaped map during wheel running and searching in an open box, recorded with calcium imaging

Obenhaus and colleagues used two-photon calcium imaging to record from the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a brain area that contains grid cells (ref. 40). Calcium imaging uses a dye that glows when a cell fires, so it shows activity as a picture. They did this in mice that were either freely moving or held still with their heads fixed. We studied three recordings from mouse 88592 (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 2a). Each had both sessions in an open box, searching for food, and sessions on a running wheel (W). We grouped the cells by their cross-correlations and found a grid cell group in each recording.

Applying our approach showed a doughnut shape in the barcode of each session (Fig. 2c and Supplementary Fig. 2b). On the wheel, we took the two longest circular features in the barcode and turned them into two angles. The activity mostly moved in one direction around the doughnut, which matches how the animal ran (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Movie 2). In the open box, the activity formed stripes that match the two repeating directions of the grid pattern (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 2c, Supplementary Movie 1).

This suggests that the brain's internal position can still add up the animal's movements and its sense of body position, even when the animal's location is not changing. On the wheel, the wheel's position relative to any landmark stays fixed. This supports the idea of path integration: that the brain works out position by adding up speed over time, rather than by finding landmarks.

Each cell also had a single tuning field on the doughnut, in the same place in the open box and on the wheel. To check this, we measured how far apart the two cells' positions were on the doughnut. We compared this with the distances from 1000 random shuffles of the data. The positions were closer than the shuffled ones (P < 0.001; Fig. 2e–g and Supplementary Fig. 2d). This shows that the internal map stays stable across tasks.

In summary, the two-dimensional doughnut-shaped map of grid cell modules carries over into very simple tasks. This suggests we can find and understand the brain's internal structure even in simple experiments where we may not have access to the cells' two-dimensional position tuning.

**Fig. 2. Uncovering a two-dimensional doughnut-shaped map in a group of grid cells during wheel running.**

**a** Obenhaus and colleagues imaged the MEC during wheel running and free searching in open boxes (ref. 40). **b** Table of how different each pair of cells is, sorted as in Fig. 1b. The relevant group ('M', 211 cells) is marked. **c** Barcodes (as in Fig. 1e) of the group's activity during free searching in an open box (left) and wheel running (right). Arrows show the pattern of a two-dimensional doughnut: one 0-dimensional bar (H0), two 1-dimensional bars (H1) and one 2-dimensional bar (H2). **d** Turning the circular features from wheel running (ϕ1,2, as in c) into angles shows one-way movement on the doughnut. Top left: the average activity of the group, colored by the 'viridis' color bar. The position of the activity bump is traced for 12 s (color bar 'hot'), in step with running on the wheel (bottom left). Right: applying the wheel's two angles to the open box session shows that they match the repeating directions of the grid pattern (similar to Fig. 1f). **e** Five examples of single cells, as in Fig. 1g. From left: tuning to two-dimensional position in space; one-dimensional position on the wheel, measured by auto-correlation; and the cell's position on the doughnut during the open box (OF) and wheel (W) sessions. **f, g** Each cell's position on the doughnut is the center of its tuning field (see e). Comparing each cell's position across wheel and open box sessions shows that its place in the internal map is stable. Positions are shown on the doughnut for the data in (b), (c) and (f), with black lines joining each cell's position in the two sessions. The bottom panel shows how the distances between positions in wheel and open box sessions are spread out for three days of recording (days #1–3), compared with shuffled data ('Sh'; g). Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

### Mouse grid cells keep the same doughnut-shaped map in virtual reality, recorded with Neuropixels

Campbell and colleagues used Neuropixels probes to record spikes from the MEC of mice whose heads were held still (ref. 14). The mice ran on a wheel in a virtual reality (VR) setup, which showed them a track. They ran under different conditions: baseline, dark, gain and contrast. In the gain condition, the wheel was slowed down compared with the VR track. In the contrast condition, the visual cues were made less sharp (Fig. 3a).

We first studied one example recording day, mouse I1 day 0417 (Fig. 3b, f–h), which gave good results. Of the 286 cells in the analysis, 101 were 'distance' or 'putative grid' cells. These were picked out by the shared repeating pattern in their one-dimensional spatial auto-correlations, as in Campbell and colleagues (Supplementary Fig. 3b and d). We then repeated our analysis on the rest of the available data (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Figs. 4–8; mouse J5 day 0505 is shown in Fig. 3b–e).

We first grouped the cells by their cross-correlations (Fig. 3b), without assuming anything about their position tuning. We found three groups, with 25, 49 and 65 cells. These contained 23, 30 and 29 distance cells, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 3b and d). Applying our approach to the firing rates of these groups gave barcodes that suggested a doughnut shape: one H0 bar, two H1 bars and one H2 bar (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 4b).

Turning the barcode into angles showed mostly one-way paths on the doughnut (Fig. 3f, g). Most cells in each group stayed within a particular area of the doughnut's surface (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Figs. 6–8). Each cell's preferred place on the doughnut stayed the same across the experimental conditions (P < 0.001 compared with 1000 shuffles; Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 4c, d). Taken together, the method found grid cell maps without the animal needing to move in two dimensions.

**Fig. 3. Revealing two-dimensional doughnut-shaped maps in groups of grid cells while the animal runs along a single straight line in virtual reality.**

**a** Campbell and colleagues used Neuropixels probes to record from the MEC while mice, with their heads held still, ran in a VR task (ref. 14). The task showed a straight track that repeated endlessly, 400 cm long, with five evenly spaced visual cues and a water reward at the end (baseline trials). **b** Tables of how different each pair of cells is (as in Fig. 1b) for two mice, with the groups marked ('M', 'M1–M3'). **c** Barcodes (as in Fig. 1e) of group M1, mouse J5 (43 cells), during baseline, contrast (changes in how sharp the visual cues were) and dark trials. **d** Four examples of single cells: one-dimensional auto-correlation on the VR track (left, 'Acorr'), and tuning to the cell's position on the doughnut during baseline (B), contrast (C) and dark (D) sessions, as in Fig. 2e. **e** Comparison of each cell's position on the doughnut between sessions for mouse J5, group M1 (as in Fig. 2f; left, 43 cells). Right: the average distance between positions for each group ('Or') with more than one session, compared with the shuffled average ('Sh'). Error bars show ± the standard error of the mean (S.E.M.), a measure of how precisely the average is known. Groups: 25 cells (I1 #2 M1), 49 (I1 #2 M2), 65 (I1 #2 M1), 46 (H3), 24 (I1 #1), 28 (J1), 43 (J5 #1), 50 (J5 #2 M1), 43 (J5 #2 M3) and 25 (J5 #3). **f** Left: the three-dimensional doughnut made from the two angles for the first third of baseline trials, for the three groups of mouse I1 (25, 49 and 65 cells, as marked in b). All parts of the doughnut seem to be visited, even though the animal runs along a straight track. Right: each module's position on the doughnut, unwrapped into a flat sheet, showing that movement across the module lines up in the dark session. **g** The animal's position on the VR track (y-axis) over time (x-axis), colored by each module's position on the doughnut, as in b (color map). Bottom: the gain (of optical flow, the brain's estimate of movement from the changing image) and contrast values during the session. **h** Violin plot of the length of the path on the doughnut for each trial, across all animals (y-axis), grouped by gain (x-axis). There were 1230 trials at gain 1, 87 at 0.8, 36 at 0.7, 23 at 0.6 and 80 at 0.5. Lengths are scaled by the average length in baseline trials. The black line shows the average. The dashed lines show the expected trial length if the path strictly followed the distance on the wheel (dark green) or on the VR track (cyan). The shading shows how the trials are spread out, and the gray lines show the range from shortest to longest. Source data are provided as a Source Data file.

Next, we grouped the remaining 118 recordings. We called a group a grid cell module if its cells' positions on the doughnut matched an idealized pattern of points on a six-sided doughnut (ref. 44; Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). This is what we would expect for grid cells (ref. 45), as shown in computer models of grid cells called continuous attractor networks (Supplementary Fig. 3a). We found the same doughnut-shaped (grid cell) features as in the groups above in 17 more groups (Supplementary Figs. 4, 3b–e and 6–8).

### The doughnut-shaped map in virtual reality shifts, but follows changes in gain and contrast

We colored the one-dimensional VR paths with the two angles from the doughnut. This showed a clear link between position in space and position on the doughnut that changed over time (Fig. 3g, Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Movie 3). Sometimes the movement on the doughnut lined up with the movement in space. In the figures, this shows up as stretches of a steady horizontal pattern. Now and then, though, the alignment would shift or drift, as Low and colleagues also suggested (ref. 46).

For the three groups in mouse I1 day 0417, this seemed to happen together, in step. This fits recent work showing that grid modules drift together in the dark (ref. 42). However, the gain and contrast changes clearly shifted how the doughnut lined up with the virtual space. When the contrast went from high to low, the lined-up map quickly disappeared. It came back once the contrast was reset to the old value.

During strong gain changes (gain = 0.5, with contrast at either 10% or 100%), the path on the doughnut was longer than in baseline sessions for 14 out of 15 groups. This was statistically significant (P < 0.05, Z > 4; Fig. 3h). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. So, in line with Campbell and colleagues (2021), the grid cells' activity seems to be shaped by two things together: the animal's own movement (seen in the dark and gain changes) and the visual cues (seen in the contrast changes).
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

We found and revealed the doughnut-shaped (torus) structure of grid cell activity in mice, using two ways of recording. One was calcium imaging, which uses a dye that glows when a cell is active. The other was electrophysiology, which records the electrical signals of cells. This two-dimensional structure shows up both while the animal's head is held still and while it runs on a wheel, which is a one-dimensional task. We saw a clear link between how the activity moves around the doughnut and how the animal moves. This suggests path integration, working out where you are by adding up your own movements.

The doughnut shape stayed the same from one recording session to the next. However, the way the activity lined up with the track in the virtual reality setup changed when we changed the brightness and contrast of the images. The alignment also shifted in a consistent way during baseline trials, the quiet trials before the animal starts a task. We also describe a three-dimensional doughnut-shaped map for groups of grid cells that respond both to position and to the direction the animal is facing. During slow-wave sleep, a deep stage of sleep, we also found a circular map in boundary vector cells, which fire when the animal is a certain distance from a wall, and another circular map in head direction cells, which fire for a particular direction the animal faces.

Our results also show, as a first proof that the idea works, how looking at the shapes in a population code lets us find groups of cells in large brain recordings. It also lets us study what those cells calculate, even in the simplest experiments (Fig. 4). This adds to a debate in fields such as the study of vision, where researchers ask whether simple, artificial setups are enough. Our results also support a wide range of experimental methods that use animals with their heads held still, either running along a single straight line or in virtual environments. These setups have several benefits. They allow experiments that record many animals quickly, even with large equipment or equipment that is sensitive to movement. They allow detailed tracking of the animal. And they allow the same analysis to be repeated in the same way on every trial. We believe these findings open the way to new insights beyond what people expected from such artificial setups, and that this may also apply to other brain regions and to more complex thinking tasks.

Fig. 4

How grid cell activity fills a two-dimensional doughnut-shaped map while the animal runs along a single straight line and in two dimensions (left and center), and during natural behavior (right).

Studying single cells in simple tasks may show that each cell responds to particular features of the behavior (top row). But the activity of all the recorded cells together is often hard to make sense of. In this case it only shows the shape of the task itself (bottom row, where the activity covers the shape of the environment). If we focus instead on particular groups of cells, such as grid cell modules, we can uncover the structure built into the brain's calculations (middle row, the doughnut-shaped map, as shown here for the one-dimensional and two-dimensional setups and during sleep). This structure is likely to carry over to natural behavior (right).

The map that grid cells make of space can look distorted in two dimensions, for example in the dark (see Supplementary Fig. 1d). In one dimension, the way the map lines up with the animal's position keeps changing. It is sensitive both to outside cues, such as landmarks, and to the animal's own sense of movement (Figs. 2, 3). This makes the properties of single cells seem hard to study, unless the animal is in a square box of the right size with reliable cues. Our results support looking at grid cells instead through their own internal doughnut shape. We propose that grid cells, and other kinds of cells with simple shapes in their activity, are best understood by looking at the space their activity fills and at how these spaces interact. Examples are head direction cells and simple cells in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that handles vision. This suggests moving away from relying on features of the task, and using ideas from topology, the branch of mathematics that studies shapes, in future studies of many different brain systems.
